4.2.1:
Why this matters

Not every relationship is a straight line. Fuel use rises faster at high speeds; error rates fall quickly with early training, then level off. Forcing a straight line onto a curve gives poor predictions and wrong conclusions about where to set an X.

The big idea

When the scatterplot or the residuals show a curve, change the model so it can bend:

  1. Add polynomial terms: a quadratic model adds X², a cubic adds X³.
Quadratic: Ŷ = b₀ + b₁X + b₂X²

A quadratic can make one bend (a U-shape or an arch); a cubic can make two.

  1. Transform X or Y: for example, use log(X) or √Y, which can straighten some curves (see 4.2.5).

How you know you need it

  • The scatterplot shows a clear bend.
  • The residuals vs fits plot from a straight-line model shows a curved pattern (4.1.3). That arch is the clearest signal.
  • After adding the X² term, its p-value is significant, the residual pattern disappears and S (typical error) drops.

Example

Fuel economy (mpg) vs speed (mph): economy improves from 45 to about 55 mph, then drops at higher speeds. A straight line through these points has a poor fit and arched residuals. A quadratic model, Ŷ = b₀ + b₁(speed) + b₂(speed)², captures the peak, and its fitted curve shows the best speed (where the curve tops out).

Higher R² is not always better

Adding terms always increases R² a little, even useless ones. A cubic or higher model may wiggle through the sample points perfectly yet predict new data badly. This is overfitting: the model fits the noise in this particular sample.

Guard against it:

  • Choose the simplest model that fits (the principle of parsimony).
  • Check that new terms are significant and that adjusted R² (and predicted R², if available) improve, not just R².
  • Make sure the curve makes physical sense for the process.

Choosing from a fitted-line plot

When an exam shows linear and quadratic fits of the same data:

  • If the points clearly curve and the quadratic term is significant (and S is lower, adjusted R² higher), choose the quadratic.
  • If the points look straight and the quadratic term is not significant, choose the linear model (simpler).

Check yourself

  1. What term turns a linear model into a quadratic one?
  2. Which residual pattern signals that a non-linear model is needed?
  3. A cubic model has R² = 0.97 and a linear model has R² = 0.95, but the cubic terms are not significant. Which do you choose?
  4. What is overfitting?
Show answers
  1. An X² (squared) term.
  2. A curve (arch or U-shape) in the residuals vs fits plot.
  3. The linear model: simpler, and the extra terms add nothing significant.
  4. A model so complex it fits the random noise in the sample and predicts new data poorly.

Key takeaways

  • Curved data: add X² (or X³), or transform.
  • Curved residuals are the main signal.
  • Higher R² is not automatically better; prefer the simplest adequate model.
4.2.2:
Why this matters

Real outputs depend on several inputs at once: delivery time depends on distance, stops, traffic and load time. Multiple regression models them together, estimates each X's effect while holding the others constant, and reveals which X's matter most. It is often the main tool for building the "Y = f(X)" model (1.1.4) in Analyze and Improve.

The big idea

Ŷ = b₀ + b₁X₁ + b₂X₂ + … + bₖXₖ

Each coefficient bᵢ is the change in Y for a one-unit increase in Xᵢ, holding all the other X's constant. That "holding constant" is what simple regression cannot do.

Example: Ŷ (delivery hours) = 1.2 + 0.018 (miles) + 0.45 (stops). Each extra stop adds 0.45 hours, for the same distance. Each extra mile adds 0.018 hours, for the same number of stops.

Testing the model

  • Overall F-test (in the ANOVA table): H₀: all slopes are zero. A small p-value means at least one X is useful. df: regression k, error n − k − 1, total n − 1.
  • Individual t-tests for each coefficient: is this X useful given the others are already in the model?
  • R²: share of variation explained by all the X's together.
  • Adjusted R²: R² penalized for the number of terms. Adding a useless X raises R² slightly but can lower adjusted R², which tells you to leave it out.
  • S: typical size of the residuals. On the IASSC sheet: S = √[Σ(Y − Ŷ)² ÷ (n − (k + 1))].

Multicollinearity

Multicollinearity occurs when the X's are correlated with each other, for example miles and fuel used, or truck age and mileage. The model cannot tell which one deserves the credit, so:

  • Coefficients become unstable: they can change a lot, or even flip sign, when data or terms change.
  • Standard errors inflate, so individual p-values look insignificant.
  • Classic symptom: the overall F-test is highly significant and R² is high, but none of the individual t-tests is significant.

Measure it with the variance inflation factor (VIF) for each X:

VIF = 1 ÷ (1 − R²ⱼ)

where R²ⱼ is the R² from regressing Xⱼ on all the other X's. VIF = 1 means no correlation with the others. If R²ⱼ = 0.8, VIF = 5. A common rule of thumb flags VIF above 5 (some use 10) as a problem; this is a convention, not an IASSC-defined cutoff. Fixes: remove one of the correlated X's, combine them, or collect data where they vary independently (a designed experiment).

Building the model

  • Backward elimination: start with all candidate X's, remove the term with the highest p-value (above α), refit, and repeat until all remaining terms are significant. This is the standard approach.
  • Stepwise: software adds and removes terms one at a time based on p-values.
  • Best subsets: software compares all combinations and reports the best models of each size by adjusted R², S and other criteria (such as Mallows' Cp, low exam yield).
  • Aim for parsimony: the fewest terms that explain Y well.

Do not drop a term on its p-value alone if it is important for the purpose (for example, a factor you control and must set).

Interactions

An interaction means the effect of one X depends on the level of another. Example: extra stops add much more time in a city than on rural routes, so "stops × urban" is an interaction term.

Ŷ = b₀ + b₁X₁ + b₂X₂ + b₃(X₁ × X₂)

Hierarchy rule: if an interaction term stays in the model, keep both of its main effects (X₁ and X₂), even if one of them has a weak p-value on its own.

Categorical predictors

X's like shift, supplier or machine are categories, not numbers. Software includes them as indicator (dummy) variables (for example, 1 if night shift, 0 if day). Each coefficient then compares that category with a baseline. You only need to recognize this, not code it by hand.

Worked example: reading output

TermCoefPVIF
Constant1.200.010
Miles0.0180.0001.3
Stops0.450.0021.3
Driver age−0.0040.6401.1

R² = 84.0%, adjusted R² = 82.1%.

  1. Miles and stops are significant (p < 0.05); driver age is not (p = 0.64).
  2. Backward elimination: remove driver age and refit. Adjusted R² will likely rise slightly.
  3. VIFs are all low, so multicollinearity is not a concern.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Each coefficient holds the other X's constant.
  • High F and R² but no significant t-tests = multicollinearity. Check VIF.
  • Adjusted R² can fall when a useless term is added.
  • Backward elimination removes the highest-p term first, one at a time.
  • Keep the main effects of any retained interaction.

Check yourself

  1. In Ŷ = 5 + 2X₁ − 3X₂, what happens to Y if X₂ increases by 1 and X₁ stays the same?
  2. An X has R²ⱼ = 0.9 when regressed on the other X's. What is its VIF, and is that a concern?
  3. Why can adjusted R² fall when a term is added?
  4. A model's interaction A×B is significant, but A alone has p = 0.3. Do you remove A?
  5. Multiple regression with n = 30 and k = 3: what are the regression, error and total df?
Show answers
  1. Y decreases by 3.
  2. VIF = 1 ÷ 0.1 = 10: a concern (above the 5 rule of thumb).
  3. Because it penalizes extra terms; a useless term adds complexity without enough explained variation.
  4. No. Keep main effects of a retained interaction (hierarchy).
  5. 3, 26, 29.

Key takeaways

  • Ŷ = b₀ + b₁X₁ + … + bₖXₖ; each b is the effect holding other X's constant.
  • Overall F, individual t-tests, R² and adjusted R².
  • Multicollinearity: correlated X's; VIF = 1 ÷ (1 − R²ⱼ); above 5 (or 10) is a warning.
  • Build by backward elimination, stepwise or best subsets; keep the model parsimonious.
  • Interactions: effect of one X depends on another; keep their main effects.
4.2.3:
Why this matters

A regression prediction is a single number, but decisions need a range. There are two different ranges, answering two different questions, and mixing them up is a classic exam trap.

The big idea

At a given value of X, the model predicts Ŷ. Two intervals can surround it:

  • Confidence interval (CI) for the mean response: the range for the average Y of all units at that X. "What is the average fuel use for all 22-ton loads?"
  • Prediction interval (PI): the range for one single new observation at that X. "How much fuel will the next 22-ton load use?"

Why the prediction interval is wider

The CI only has to account for uncertainty about where the line is (sampling error in b₀ and b₁). The PI must account for that plus the scatter of individual points around the line (the residual variation). Individual values vary much more than averages, so the prediction interval is always wider.

Both bands are narrowest at the mean of X and widen toward the ends of the data.

Narrowest at the center

Both intervals are narrowest at X̄ (the mean of the X data) and widen as X moves away from it. The model is most certain in the middle of its data and least certain near the edges, and beyond the data (extrapolation) the uncertainty grows fast.

Choosing the right interval

Wording cues:

  • "the average delivery time for 300-mile trips", "the mean output at X = 10" → confidence interval.
  • "the next truck", "a single new unit", "this one shipment" → prediction interval.

Example

Software output at load weight = 22 tons:

  • Fit: 17.68 gallons per 100 miles.
  • 95% CI: 16.8 to 18.6 (the average for all 22-ton loads).
  • 95% PI: 15.6 to 19.8 (the next individual 22-ton load).

For setting a fuel budget across many loads, use the CI. For promising a customer a range for one load, use the PI.

Check yourself

  1. Which interval is used for a single future unit?
  2. Why is the prediction interval wider?
  3. Where along X are the intervals narrowest?
  4. "What will the average cycle time be for all orders of 50 lines?" Which interval?
Show answers
  1. The prediction interval.
  2. It includes the scatter of individual values around the line, not just uncertainty about the line itself.
  3. At the mean of X (X̄).
  4. The confidence interval for the mean response.

Key takeaways

  • CI: the mean response at X. PI: one new observation at X.
  • PI is always wider than CI.
  • Both narrowest at X̄, wider toward the edges; do not extrapolate.
4.2.4:
The big idea

Multiple regression rests on the same assumptions as simple regression (4.1.3): linearity, independence, constant variance and normal residuals. The same four residual plots check them: normal probability plot, histogram, residuals vs fits, residuals vs order. The same patterns mean the same problems: a funnel means non-constant variance, a curve means a missing term, a pattern over order means a time effect.

With several X's, add these checks:

Residuals vs each X

Plot residuals against each predictor separately. A curve against one particular X shows exactly which variable needs a squared term or a transformation.

Multicollinearity (VIF)

Check the VIF of each predictor (4.2.2). High VIFs make coefficients unstable and p-values unreliable.

Leverage and influence

With several X's, a point can be unusual in a combination of X values even if each value looks normal on its own (a short trip with an unusually large number of stops). Software flags:

  • High leverage: points with unusual X combinations (large "hat" values).
  • Large standardized residuals: points the model fits badly (often beyond ±2 or ±3).
  • Cook's distance: combines leverage and residual size to measure how much each point influences the fitted coefficients. Points with large Cook's distance deserve investigation.

Interpreting a full four-pack

Typical exam reasoning:

  • Normal plot straight, histogram bell-shaped, residuals vs fits random, residuals vs order random → assumptions met; trust the p-values and intervals.
  • Normal plot curved and residuals vs fits funneled → transform Y (Box-Cox, 4.2.5), then refit and recheck.
  • Residuals vs fits arched → add a squared term for the X that shows the curve.
  • Residuals vs order trending → look for a time-related variable (wear, learning, season) and consider adding it.
  • One point far from the rest with large Cook's distance → check the data; if real, analyze with and without it and report both.

Check yourself

  1. What extra plot helps find which X needs a squared term?
  2. What does Cook's distance measure?
  3. Residuals funnel and the normal plot bends. What is the first fix to try?
Show answers
  1. Residuals vs each individual X.
  2. How much a single point influences the fitted model (combining leverage and residual size).
  3. Transform Y (for example with Box-Cox), refit and recheck.

Key takeaways

  • Same four residual checks as simple regression.
  • Add residuals vs each X, VIF, leverage, standardized residuals and Cook's distance.
  • Diagnose, fix (transform or add terms), refit, recheck.
4.2.5:
Why this matters

Many tools assume normal data or constant variance. Real data (times, costs, counts) are often skewed, with spread growing as values grow. A transformation re-expresses the data on a different scale where those assumptions hold, so the standard tools work.

The big idea

A transformation applies the same mathematical function to every data point: take the square root, the logarithm, or the reciprocal. Skewed data with a long right tail often become close to normal on a log scale, because the log compresses large values more than small ones.

Box-Cox transformations

The Box-Cox method searches a family of power transformations, Y raised to a power λ (lambda), and finds the λ that makes the data most nearly normal with constant variance:

λTransformation
2Y² (square)
1Y (no transformation)
0.5√Y (square root)
0ln(Y) (natural log), by definition
−0.51 ÷ √Y
−11 ÷ Y (reciprocal)

(For λ = 0, Y⁰ would be 1 for every value, which is useless, so the natural log is used instead; it is the mathematical limit of the family.)

Reading Box-Cox output

Software reports:

  • The optimal λ (best estimate).
  • A confidence interval for λ.
  • A rounded λ to use in practice.

Rules:

  • If the CI for λ includes 1, no transformation may be needed (λ = 1 means "leave the data alone"), even if the optimal λ is not exactly 1.
  • Otherwise, pick a rounded, interpretable λ inside the CI: 0.5 (square root), 0 (log), −1 (reciprocal). A log is often chosen when 0 is inside the interval, because log scales are easy to explain.

Example: optimal λ = 0.12, 95% CI −0.20 to 0.45. The CI excludes 1 (transform) and includes 0, so use the natural log.

Requirements and cautions

  • Box-Cox needs positive data. If there are zeros or negative values, add a constant first so all values are positive.
  • When using transformed data for capability (2.4), transform the specification limits the same way, or the comparison is meaningless.
  • Results on the transformed scale (means, intervals) should be converted back to the original units when reporting to people.
  • Transforming is not always the answer: if non-normality comes from mixed populations or outliers, fix that cause instead (2.2.3).

Other options

The Johnson transformation is a more flexible alternative that can handle data Box-Cox cannot. Recognition only.

Check yourself

  1. Which λ means "no transformation"?
  2. Which transformation corresponds to λ = 0?
  3. Box-Cox gives λ = 0.6 with CI 0.3 to 1.1. What do you do?
  4. The data include zeros. What must you do before Box-Cox?
  5. After log-transforming cycle times for a capability study, what else must be transformed?
Show answers
  1. λ = 1.
  2. The natural log.
  3. The CI includes 1, so a transformation may not be needed; if one is used, λ = 0.5 (square root) is a reasonable rounded choice.
  4. Add a constant so all values are positive.
  5. The specification limits.

Key takeaways

  • Transformations re-express data to make it more normal or the variance more constant.
  • Box-Cox λ: 1 = none, 0.5 = square root, 0 = log, −1 = reciprocal.
  • If λ's CI includes 1, maybe no transform; otherwise pick a rounded λ in the CI.
  • Needs positive data; transform spec limits too for capability.
